text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The Swedish state is on collision course with insurer Skandia and mortgage bank Stadshypotek after the two companies proposed a merger on Monday. Finance Minister Erik Asbrink expressed strong opposition to the merger and wants to get the best possible price for the sale of the state's 34 percent stake in Stadshypotek.

- A court of appeal ruled in favoiur of a man whose insurance compoany had said that the alcohol level in his blood constituted careless driving. A doctor however testified that the man, who is seeking compensation from the insurance company, had 1.73 promilles of alcohol in his blood but had developed an alcohol tolerance.

- Swedish bank Handelsbanken produces the most optimistic forecasts to date for the Swedish economy, saying economic growth is expected within the coming year. The bank's economist forecast Gross Domestic Product rising by 2.9 percent in 1997 and 2.7 percent in 1998, driving by rising private consumption.
- Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink gets into full stride to oppose a merger between insurer Skandia and mortgage bank Stadshypotek that is 34 percent owned by the state.
- More Swedes are on their way to the Comoro Islands to join the search for two female public servants missing after a hijacked plane crashed off the coast.

- Seven neo-Nazis from the National Socialist Front who were allegedly involved in a riot during a demonstration in Trollhattan in August are in court to answer charges of threatening minority groups. The seven, aged between 17 and 21, were part of a demonstration to mark the anniversary of the death of Rudolf Hess, Hitler's deputy.

- Swedish insurer Skandia and mortgage bank Stadshypotek announced they wanted to merge to become the leading financial institution in the Nordic region with total assets of 500 billion crowns. But Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink sharply criticised the plan and said he had no confidence in the current board of Stadshypotek. He said other companies will have the chance to bid for the state's 34 percent holding of the mortgage bank.

- International engineering roup ABB wins contracts worth $00 million to equip nuclear power plants in South Korea as well as a turnkey contract valued at $100 million to build Indonesia's first combined cycle power plant.

- Ericsson signed a three-year agreement with Britain's Vodafone to supply equipment worth over $330 million as part of the operator's strategy of providing innovative services to corporate customers.

- Cash-rich firms in Sweden, Germany and Switzerland are likely to turn increasingly to company buybacks as a means to redistribute shareholder wealth, according to a study by JP Morgan Securitieis Ltd. In Sweden 13 companies were identified including Ericsson, Hennes & Mauritz, Kinnevik, Volvo, Astra, Skanska and all the large forestry firms.
